editorNote: Comdex/Spring packs Atlanta with IBM-compatible machines and integrated software, while Framework, multiuser PCs and dial-up security show where the market is heading.
morningLine: Monday, May 28, 1984: 851 suppliers crowd Comdex/Spring as personal computing’s boom widens.

lead.headline: Comdex/Spring Shows the Micro Market Still Surging
lead.dek: Atlanta fills with 851 suppliers, IBM-compatible machines and a new contest to put every office task inside one package.
body: Comdex/Spring opened on a scale that made the personal-computer boom impossible to miss. Computerworld counted 851 suppliers, 158 of them first-time exhibitors, and expected well over 45,000 visitors. The aisles offered a working map of an industry still multiplying around the IBM PC standard.

IBM PCs and compatible machines dominated the floor. Corona introduced its 8088-based Personal Best, including a $5,995 configuration with 512KB of memory, twin 5.25-inch floppy drives and a 10MB hard disk. TeleVideo showed its Telecolor PC, while Morrow’s nine-pound Pivot portable used a low-power 80C86 and a compact LCD.

The strongest crowds gathered around integrated software. Ashton-Tate’s Framework and Lotus Symphony promised to bring writing, calculation, graphics and data together, reducing the friction of passing office work among separate programs.

Apple’s Macintosh kept a lower profile, with hardware add-ons visible but relatively few applications on display. For this week, the market’s center of gravity remained the expanding family of IBM-compatible micros—and the software makers racing to make them more coherent.

stories.headline: Framework Bets $695 That Ideas Belong in an Outline
body: Ashton-Tate’s Framework combines an outline editor, word processor, spreadsheet, graph generator, database manager and the Fred programming language in a $695 IBM PC package. It requires 256KB and two floppy drives.

Its unusual promise is fluid movement among kinds of work: a spreadsheet cell can contain a document, graphs and sheets can enter prose, and database results can become charts. Pull-down menus and keyboard commands provide the controls without requiring a mouse.

Developer Robert C.M. Carr argues that people do not think linearly. Framework makes that claim concrete by arranging material in nested outlines and movable frames, while Fred’s roughly 140 verbs open the package to customization.

stories.headline: Delayed Windows Leaves PC Software on Islands
body: At a Comdex session, consultant Esther Dyson warned that DOS programs still lacked a common operating environment linking integrated packages to one another. Shared interfaces and dependable data transfer, she argued, mattered as much as each suite’s growing list of features.

Microsoft Windows had missed its announced April shipment date, leaving developers to pursue separate answers. Dyson pointed to Visi On, Lotus Symphony add-ins and Quarterdeck’s Desq as competing approaches rather than one settled standard.

The Macintosh showed the other path: Apple’s prescribed environment restricted developers but gave users consistent behavior. On the PC, the abundance visible at Comdex also exposed the cost of fragmentation.

stories.headline: TeleVideo Puts PCs Around an $8,995 Multiuser Hub
body: TeleVideo’s PM/16 proposes a shared center for IBM-compatible offices before IBM delivers its own microcomputer network. The 8MHz 80186 system includes 256KB of memory, a 46MB hard disk and the Infoshare operating system.

Connected PCs can keep running local applications while sharing central data, programs and printers. Infoshare supplies file and record locking, print spooling, online help and a hierarchical multiuser file system.
The $8,995 hub is due at the end of June, with adapters priced at $199 per PC. TeleVideo believes it has a two- to three-year opening in which to establish the idea.

bbsNote.headline: CompuServe Presses for Anti-Hacker Laws as Dial-Up Abuse Grows
bbsNote.summary: At the Information Industry Association's Boston meeting, CompuServe vice president George Minot said unauthorized callers could steal services and occupy scarce ports; Massachusetts aide Jonathan Winer outlined a bill criminalizing intentional access and data theft or damage.

posts.text: Minot said one intrusion consumed a million dollars' worth of CompuServe services in two days, and urged providers to strengthen security, consult law enforcement before incidents, and display explicit no-trespassing notices. Computerworld reported a proposed Massachusetts misdemeanor penalty of up to one year in jail and a $5,000 fine for intentional intrusion, with felony treatment for data larceny.

The June 1984 Timelinez guide documented a real user-group path onto CompuServe: Timex/Sinclair owners could use the CEM 450 Special Interest Group to read messages and exchange information, illustrating how machine-specific communities were forming inside national services.

curiosity.headline: The Nine-Pound Portable with a Sixteen-Line Window
curiosity.summary: Morrow's Pivot compressed an MS-DOS computer into nine pounds, but its LCD showed only 16 rows of 80 characters.
curiosity.detail: The Comdex machine used Harris's low-power 80C86, shipped with 128KB RAM expandable to 512KB, and started below $2,500—an unusually vivid snapshot of the compromises behind 1984 portability.

gadgetWatch.headline: The Television Becomes an Electronic Playpen
gadgetWatch.summary: TIME's May 28 cover-date feature described households assembling TVs, cable, VCRs, videodisc players, stereos, and game machines into integrated entertainment centers—an exact-week consumer-electronics snapshot.
